extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and readers interested in politics, morality, and the French Revolution (late 18th-century British readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A moral and political critique arguing that 'Illumination' (the Illuminati/Enlightenment-inspired factions) undermined religion and morality and helped drive the French Revolution; offers prescriptive maxims about prudence in speculation and public conduct. Includes narrative evidence and reflections intended to guide public judgment and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack on Morality and Religion as the first tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: “in all those villainous machinations against the peace of the world, the attack has been first made on the principles of Morality and Religion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conspirators target religious and moral principles initially because they consider religion and morality inseparably connected; by undermining these principles they remove the main restraints on popular behaviour, facilitating later political subversion. (Context: author urges readers to note this pattern in revolutionary activity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Destroy religious sentiments by corrupting morals
rubrics_metrics.description: “They endeavour to destroy our religious sentiments, by first corrupting our morals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include inflaming passions and presenting religious restraints as inventions of priests and despots; once passions are enlisted, those persuaded will not further interrogate causes. The text treats this as a deliberate, staged method used to prepare populations for political change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against having judgments warped by desires
rubrics_metrics.description: “guard ourselves with the most anxious care against the risk of having our judgments warped by our desires.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are instructed to be truly rational—use experience to check speculative impulses, especially on passion-engaging subjects. The author advocates self-examination to prevent wishful thinking from determining belief and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of wild and extravagant speculation (Illumination)
rubrics_metrics.description: “there are also times of wild and extravagant speculation... The present day... is gloried in as the prerogative of the eighteenth century.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative enthusiasm, when widespread, tends to lessen moral restraints and lead to social disorder. The author counsels moderation in speculative indulgence and skepticism toward claims that speculative 'illumination' is inherently virtuous or socially beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject as instructors those who display dishonesty or degraded conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: “Such men are unsuitable instructors... he sees plain proofs of degraded self estimation, of dishonesty, and of mean motives.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prudent person should refuse to take moral or political instruction from clergy or others who act contrary to their professed oaths or who show parasitic or dishonest motives—honesty admits of no degrees; an instructor who is a knave is untrustworthy regardless of rhetorical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason alone is insufficient for governing masses; religious sanctions underpin public morality
rubrics_metrics.description: “How will a whole nation act when religious sanctions are removed, and men are actuated by reason alone?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoic-style reasoned virtue may suit exceptional individuals but cannot replace religious sanctions for the general population; the author points to events in revolutionary France (e.g., decrees affecting sexual morality) as evidence that removing religious restraints produces social degradation and disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illumination fosters self-conceit while destroying grounds for self-estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are abundantly self-conceited; and yet they continually endeavour to destroy all grounds of self-estimation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author critiques Enlightenment/Illuminati tendencies to celebrate discoveries that reduce human dignity (e.g., mechanistic accounts of mind), producing both arrogance in leaders and a cultural project that undermines personal worth and moral pride among the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary policy: annihilate privileges and supplant old authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted report: “THE ANNIHILATION OF ALL PRIVILEGES, WAR WITH THE PALACES, PEACE WITH THE COTTAGES.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Convention's reported principles aim to abolish nobility, tithes, feudal rights, and other privileged orders and to replace existing authorities with a popular system—implemented aggressively (e.g., decrees translated and dispersed; constitutions imposed by occupying armies). The author uses this as evidence of a systematic, confrontational revolutionary program rather than a spontaneous popular movement.
